title: Healthy Meal Planning
summary: Check your week → Pick meals → Shop the gaps → Store leftovers safely
subtitle: Make room for meals that fit your week, your kitchen and your budget.

blocks.text: The daily question “What’s for dinner?” has impressive staying power. A meal-planning app may offer seventeen colour-coded tabs, but dinner still needs somewhere to happen. A small plan starts with the food and time you have.
Spend less, waste less and stress less about dinner.
blocks.detail: A short, flexible plan gives you a head start on busy days and helps you use the food you bring home.
blocks.extra: Section 05 gives you a three-day plan with a matching shopping list.

blocks.text: Meal planning means choosing some meals before hunger and a busy evening choose for you. It can cover two dinners, a few work lunches or a whole week. The right size is the one you can manage.

Canada’s food guide suggests filling half your plate with vegetables and fruit, a quarter with whole grains and a quarter with protein foods, choosing plant proteins more often. These are proportions, not fixed serving sizes, and they work for a bowl or a shared dish too. The guide’s free website, food-guide.canada.ca, also has budget-friendly recipes and planning tips.

This lesson offers general examples, not a personal nutrition plan. Food allergies, swallowing needs and medical eating plans need their own changes. A registered dietitian can help you adapt meals to your situation and the foods you can get.
Look at your week and mark when you can cook. Include meals someone else provides. Think about breakfast, lunch and snacks too, even if you only plan dinners at first.

Check your fridge and cupboards before you choose recipes. An open bag of carrots might fit two dinners, and a favourite sauce can make a familiar meal easier. Check that you have the pot, storage space and cooking method a recipe needs.

Match the meal to your kitchen. If you have a microwave but no stove, choose ready-cooked grains, canned beans and vegetables you can prepare as the package says. Follow the cooking directions on frozen vegetables, since not all of them are ready to eat.
Choose meals you enjoy, including foods from your own traditions. A bean stew or vegetable curry can be a starting point. Change the vegetables or grain as needed.

Write the shopping items beside each meal, then cross out what you already have. Compare shelf prices and package sizes for the amount you can use. A bigger bag only helps if you can afford it, carry it and store the extra.
Give every fresh item a job. If you buy cabbage for a rice bowl, plan a cabbage slaw for the next dinner. Repeating one ingredient can reduce waste without making every meal taste the same.

items.title: “Healthy meal planning requires fresh food and cooking everything from scratch.”
items.text: Frozen vegetables and canned foods can be part of healthy eating. Choose options that fit your money, time and storage. Rinsing canned beans and vegetables cuts some of the salt.

blocks.text: Keep an easy backup meal for schedule changes, like whole-grain toast with canned beans and carrots. Takeout or a shared meal can fit your week too. Adjust the next meal as needed.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: The Thursday lunch

blocks.text: The Thursday lunch
paragraphs: Elise taught grade six in Ottawa and wanted a lunch she could eat before her afternoon class. Her lunch break often vanished into photocopier jams and last-minute questions. She was tired of buying food on Sunday and finding it unused on Friday.

One Monday, a leaky container soaked her lesson notes, and the staff-room microwave had an Out of Order sign. Her big soup plan suddenly needed a better container and a working microwave. She bought lunch and went home with a clear problem to solve.

Elise looked at her week: a Thursday evening meeting, one small fridge shelf and no reliable way to heat lunch at school. She opened five new recipes, then closed every tab. She chose two dinners she already knew how to make and one cold lunch that used some of the same food.

On Tuesday she made chickpea rice bowls with cabbage and carrots. She put the extra in the fridge right away, labelled it and planned to eat it the next day. For Thursday, she bought whole-grain wraps and packed vegetables separately, with canned chickpeas she opened that morning.

On Wednesday came news that the staff fridge would be unplugged for repairs. Elise adjusted again. She packed her wrap in an insulated lunch bag with ice packs, and put a reminder by her keys so the bag wouldn’t stay on the counter.

Thursday’s lunch was ordinary, which was exactly what she needed. She ate it without waiting for a microwave and used the last of the cabbage at dinner. The next weekend she kept the same small plan and bought a container that sealed properly. Her lesson notes stayed dry, and the photocopier stayed the machine with problems.

blocks.text: A cold lunch still needs safe storage. Use a fridge or an insulated bag with ice packs for foods that spoil. If you can’t keep a meal cold, choose something shelf-stable instead.
Plan for your real kitchen and schedule, and a simple meal survives a change of plans.
blocks.detail: A backup that fits your storage and your week keeps you eating well when things go sideways.
blocks.extra: Section 05 walks you through a small plan you can copy.

blocks.text: This three-day dinner example is for one adult with a stove, fridge and basic utensils. Change the amounts for your appetite and household, and swap foods for allergies or tastes. Shopping amounts are starting points, not set portions.
Example: Tuesday to Thursday

items.title: Tuesday: chickpea and vegetable rice bowls. Cook brown rice using package directions; heat chickpeas with cabbage, carrots and frozen peas. Set aside Wednesday’s portion before eating.
Wednesday: reheat the reserved bowl and add fresh cabbage slaw with lemon and oil. Use the safely stored portion within the leftovers window below.
Thursday: whole grain pasta with canned tomatoes, lentils and frozen vegetables. Cook only the amount you need, or label and promptly store any extra.

blocks.text: Matching shopping list

items.title: Produce: one small cabbage, three carrots and one lemon.
Frozen: one bag of mixed vegetables or peas, used in both cooked meals.
Cupboard: one can each of chickpeas, lentils and tomatoes; small packages of brown rice and whole grain pasta.
Check at home: cooking oil, water and your preferred seasonings. Buy only what is missing.

blocks.text: Set aside about ten minutes to check your supplies and write your list. Allow the cooking time on the rice or pasta package, plus time to wash and cut vegetables. Your kitchen may take longer. For breakfast and lunch, add your usual foods to the list, like oats, fruit and yogurt, in amounts you’ll use.
In winter, longer-lasting cabbage and frozen vegetables can save money. Swap in local, seasonal vegetables when they fit your budget. You don’t need any special imported food for this plan.

Put leftovers in the fridge within two hours, in shallow containers. Let hot food stop steaming first. Keep your fridge at 4°C or colder. Eat leftovers within two to three days, or freeze them for later, and date each container.

Reheat leftovers to 74°C, checked with a digital food thermometer. Stir food while it reheats in the microwave so the heat spreads evenly. Reheat only what you’ll eat, and don’t reheat the same leftovers twice.

items.title: “A good smell proves leftovers are safe.”
items.text: Smell can’t confirm that food is safe. Throw out cooked food left at room temperature for more than two hours, and don’t taste it to check.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Put a “use first” note beside the next meal. If plans change, check the date on the label before you decide what to eat or freeze. If your freezer is full, cook smaller batches.
Quick Check

items.title: Do food guide fractions tell everyone an exact serving amount?
What should you check before adding ingredients to your list?
items.detail: Check what you have and what your kitchen can store and prepare.

items.title: How long should refrigerated leftovers be kept before eating or freezing?
items.detail: Eat them within two to three days, or freeze them for later.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: You have carrots at home and a busy evening ahead. Which plan fits? A. Buy ingredients for a long new recipe. · B. Use the carrots in a familiar quick meal. · C. Skip planning until the shop closes.
items.text: A familiar meal can use food you own and fit the time available. The recipe needs to match the evening.

items.title: Your plan requires a large frozen batch, but your freezer is full. What helps? A. Make smaller batches. · B. Keep every meal in the fridge all week. · C. Leave containers on the counter.
items.text: Smaller batches fit your storage. A weekly calendar does not extend safe storage time.

items.title: Cooked rice sat on the counter for four hours. What should you do? A. Taste a spoonful. · B. Reheat it and assume it is safe. · C. Discard it.
items.text: Four hours exceeds the two-hour limit. Discard the rice.

items.title: Describe one dinner and the shopping items you would need after checking your supplies.
items.text: Lentil pasta with tomatoes and vegetables. I have pasta and oil, so I will buy canned lentils, canned tomatoes and frozen vegetables. Your foods can differ.

blocks.text: Choose meals that fit your week, connect them to a realistic shopping list and give leftovers a safe storage plan.
Write your own small plan using the questions below. Choose a step you’re ready to try. You can change it after you see how the week goes.
Review your plan and circle your first step.

items.title: Meal plan
items.text: Meals chosen ahead for part of your week.

items.title: Proportion
items.text: The share of a meal made up by a food group.

items.title: Whole grain
items.text: Grain food containing all parts of the grain.

items.title: Plant protein
items.text: Protein food from plants, such as beans or lentils.

items.title: Leftovers
items.text: Prepared food saved for another meal.

items.title: Shelf-stable
items.text: Food safely stored without refrigeration until opened, following its label.
